title: What is Proof-of-Work?
transcript_text: If Bitcoin is fully decentralized, how can transactions be moved between users? Who selects where transactions go and how they get there? Bitcoin uses what is called a proof-of-work consensus mechanism to create agreement on where transactions go across the network. A consensus mechanism is a way to make a group of people form a collective decision. There's many consensus mechanisms in computer science. Proof-of-work was chosen for Bitcoin because it bestudes Bitcoin's radical innovation of linking computers and money. The mechanism requires anyone who wants to move Bitcoin from point A to point B to submit work to the network or pay a fee for someone to do it on their behalf. This work is called mining. Miners must expend energy to solve a puzzle of sorts that allows them to add blocks to the blockchain. After it's complete, the work of solving new blocks can easily be verified by other users. With digital work, Bitcoin effectively creates a form of artificial cost in a usually costless digital world. Anyone wishing to amend or alter the blockchain's transaction record must complete expensive work that's also trivially easy for others to verify. With the cost of proof-of-work comes the benefit of security. Proof-of-work serves as a real cost to create a new Bitcoin and a protection mechanism against bad actors who might try to alter the blockchain's transaction record. Bitcoin users can trust that the network's transaction record is valid because only values that miners have expended energy on can make it into the Bitcoin larger. Any attempt to replace or alter previous transactions requires an equivalent amount of work used to create the transaction plus the work dedicated to all the other transactions stacked below in the blockchain. In other words, an attacker would have to burn enormous amounts of energy to rewrite past transactions.
